RE:    Georgia Power Company Annual Transmission Update Report; Docket No. 56002


Dear Ms. Tanner:

In accordance with the Order Adopting Stipulation issued by the Georgia Public Service
Commission (the “Commission”) in the above-styled docket, Georgia Power Company hereby
files its Annual Transmission Update Report with the status of each transmission project in the
Company’s Selected Supporting Information contained within Technical Appendix Volume 1 and
the Unit Retirement Study contained within Technical Appendix Volume 3 of the 2025 IRP.

The Report contains certain information that is being filed under the trade secret rules of the
Commission. As such, a redacted version of this information and the basis for the trade secret
assertion are also enclosed for public disclosure.

Please contact Cheryl Johnson at 404-506-6837 if you have any questions regarding this filing.

Sincerely,


/s/ Jeremiah Haswell

Jeremiah Haswell
Director, Regulatory Affairs
Georgia Power Company
jhaswell@southernco.com

                    I.      GA INTEGRATED TRANSMISSION SYSTEM (ITS) EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

The results of the studies performed on the GA ITS demonstrate that required performance criteria are met,
or a project or operating guide has been developed to address any identified system deficiencies.
A summary of Georgia ITS Transmission additions starts on the next page, followed by the list of the Georgia
ITS 10-Year Expansion Plan Projects.
This group of projects and operating guides, found in Section IV ANALYSIS RESULTS, is reassessed annually to
confirm continued need, timing, and scope for previously identified projects until projects have transitioned
from planning to a committed project. These reassessments also identify any new potential projects needed
or modification to projects currently included. Any operating guides identified to address constraints are
reviewed by Georgia Power Company’s Transmission Operations team. The transmission improvements are
submitted to the ITS Participants for inclusion in the ITS parity process.
The following information is included for each project:
    1) project justification,
    2) implementation schedule (start date), and
    3) expected required in-service date.

For transmission improvements, lead times necessary to implement plans are considered to ensure the
expected required in-service date can be met.

                                    II.     TRANSMISSION PLANNING PROCESS DESCRIPTION

A. Annual Planning Process and Base Cases
Southern Company Services (SCS) conducts an iterative Transmission Planning process for the 10-year
planning horizon. This process ensures Georgia Integrated Transmission System (ITS) Participants receive all
necessary information to address identified system limitations. It enables them to develop projects that
comply with NERC planning standards and align with each participant’s budget and scheduling requirements.
The ITS Joint Committee for Planning and Operations determines which ITS Participant will assume
construction and ownership responsibilities, considering factors such as facility ownership and the ITS parity
forecast.

This report summarizes planning studies conducted by SCS specifically for the Georgia ITS in its role as
Planning Coordinator (PC) and Transmission Planner (TP). These studies follow the Guidelines for Planning
Transmission System Facility Improvements and are consistent with the NERC TPL-001-5 Standard
(“Standard”).

The following sections provide an overview of maintaining system models, the detailed studies performed,
which includes steady state, stability, and short circuit studies, and the resulting Projects and Operating
Guides for the mitigation of identified system deficiencies.


Maintaining System Models
The base cases include the following [Requirement 1]: Detailed studies are performed using transmission
system models (“base cases”) that are updated annually to reflect the current 10-year forecast for load and
generation within the Southern Balancing Authority Area (SBAA). These base cases use data consistent with
the NERC MOD-032 standard and are supplemented by other sources as needed, including items from the
Corrective Action Plan (CAP) and projected system conditions. Each base case also incorporates the latest
available external representation of the Eastern Interconnection, typically obtained from the Multi-Regional
Modeling Working Group (MMWG) or the SERC Reliability Corporation (SERC) Long-Term Study Group.

In accordance with [Requirement 1], the base cases include:
    1. Existing facilities.
    2. Known outages of generation or transmission facilities lasting at least six months. All such outages in
       the near-term Transmission Planning horizon are modeled with the impacted equipment out of
       service, as described in Attachment 1 of the MOD-032 Standard.
    3. New planned facilities and changes to existing facilities, rated per NERC Reliability Standard FAC-008-3.
    4. Real and reactive load forecasts provided by each Load Serving Entity within the SBAA.
    5. Known commitments for Firm Transmission Service and Interchange.
    6. Resources required to serve load.

Generation
Another key modeling assumption made in case development is the generation resources. Future generation
assumptions for native load resources for Southern Company, GTC, MEAG, and Dalton are shown in the table
in Section VI Generation Assumptions. This table lists both owned units and Power Purchase Agreements for
all parties at the beginning of the year. The dispatch program first commits sufficient resources to meet load
and reserve requirements for each company in each base case or unit-out scenario. It then adjusts generator
output levels in the most economical manner.

Normal Open Points
The ITS evaluates normal open point configurations on the Summer Cases. Some loads with radial service have
alternative transmission paths that can be used if the primary path is out of service. These alternative paths
cannot remain closed while the primary path is also closed because the resulting configuration would
compromise system protection and could create network load flow constraints.
If a change to a normal open point is requested, Operations and Planning will review the proposed
configuration to confirm that the system can accommodate the change before reconfiguration occurs.

                                                         III.     PERFORMANCE CRITERIA

A. Steady State Analysis
Steady state analyses were conducted to address TPL-001-5 Table 1 Category P0–P7 Planning Events and
Extreme Events for both near-term and long-term planning horizons. These evaluations included peak and off-
peak loading models. The System Peak loading model represents summer conditions. System Shoulder loading
models represent 85% of summer peak demand, with hydro generation motoring off-line, and include
scenarios where solar facilities are either on or off-line. This load assumption was anticipated to result in the
highest system stress outside of a full summer peak scenario, as many energy-limited resources were
projected to be off-line. Additionally, System Off-Peak cases representing 70% of the summer peak demand
were evaluated. All System Peak, Shoulder, and Off-Peak cases are evaluated using Rate B (95°F ambient
temperature) in accordance with [Requirement 2 Parts 2.1.1, 2.1.2, and 2.2.1].
A Hot Weather case representing 107% of system peak was also evaluated under ITS procedures using Rate A
(104°F ambient temperature) for all equipment ratings.
Based on these analyses, all projects required to address identified deficiencies have been added to Section
IV-E, Steady State Project Details.
Table 6 Steady State Transmission Planning Criteria below provides an overview of the methodology used to
meet TPL-001-5 Table 1 contingency requirements:

Where Table 6 Steady State Transmission Planning Criteria required a generation outage as a portion of the
contingency, a summary of key unit outs considered was developed and can be found in Section VI B,
Generation Assumptions. This table identifies the units considered and the cases in which they were applied.
Some outages were unnecessary in certain cases because the unit was already off-line due to expected
dispatch. These generating units, which impose greater stress on the system, have been identified through
years of power flow analysis based on factors such as size, location, and system impact.

Steady State Sensitivity Analysis
The standard requires sensitivity studies to demonstrate the impact of changes to base-case assumptions. The
selected sensitivity was the availability of hydroelectric generation, evaluated using TPL-001-5 Table 1 criteria.
Analyses were performed for all years in the Near-Term and Long-Term Planning Horizons under off-peak
conditions with hydro generation available and under System Shoulder conditions (85% of system peak) with
hydro generation unavailable. [Requirement 2 Part 2.1.4]

Steady State Equipment Sparing Analysis
The Transmission Equipment Sparing Strategy is reviewed annually to identify transmission equipment
without a spare and with a replacement lead time greater than one year. Each piece of equipment was
individually modeled as unavailable and evaluated for P0, P1, and P2 events using system peak, off-peak, and
the sensitivity cases. [Requirement 2 Part 2.1.5]

B. Stability Analysis
Stability studies were conducted to consider P1 - P7 Planning Events and Extreme Events in the Near-Term
planning horizon. Simulations were conducted for system peak load and off-peak load (approximately 50% of
peak) for one of the five Near-Term years. System Peak cases included a dynamic load model representing
expected induction motor behavior. The light load level of 50% of peak was chosen as a worst-case scenario
for angular stability because base-load units operate at maximum output.
All projects resulting from the stability analysis to address any identified deficiencies have been added to the
list of projects in Section IV B, Stability Project Details.

Stability Sensitivity Analysis (Near-Term Planning Horizon)
Requirement R2.4.3 of the Standard requires additional sensitivity studies to demonstrate the effects of
various modeling assumptions. For the system stability studies completed using the standard base case, the
following sensitivities were evaluated:

    •     For 50% System peak load cases, local generation was increased to maximum output.
    •     For System peak load cases, the percentage of induction motor load that was modeled at each bus
          with a dynamic load model was increased.

For studies evaluating area generator output sensitivity, generator output was modified beyond the base
dispatch, dispatching all generation near the study area at full output, whether the unit had firm service for
full output or not. This approach produced the most conservative results; therefore, no additional sensitivities
were required. The sensitivity analysis revealed no new constraints. [Requirement R2.4.3]

Steady State Coordination with Adjacent Systems
In addition to contingencies on the GA ITS system, contingencies provided by neighboring systems are
analyzed annually in accordance with TPL-001-5 Requirement 3.4.1. Neighboring systems are monitored
during all studies to determine if ITS contingencies could impact them. If potential impacts are identified, the
affected neighbor is notified per the requirement.

Long-Term Stability Analysis
Stability studies were also conducted as needed in the Long-Term planning horizon to address the impact of
material generation additions or changes in that time frame. Forecasted generation in the Long-Term
transmission planning horizon that does not have firm service or has not been designated by an entity does
not require a stability study. Only new generation with a firm commitment to build requires a unit-specific
stability study. [Requirement 2.5]

C. Short Circuit Analysis
The short circuit (breaker duty) assessment was performed by Southern Company Services Protection &
Control Applications for the Near-Term planning horizon. The base case model used for this assessment
included all existing facilities (transmission and generation) and planned facilities based on forecasted
generation and future years’ transmission expansion plan. The real and reactive load forecasts and known
commitments for Firm Transmission Service and Interchange were not represented in the models as they were
not relevant to this assessment. The methodology uses the Siemens APA “Advanced Protection Assessment”
Short Circuit Analysis program to calculate the margin between fault interrupting device capability and short
circuit levels. Short circuit currents are evaluated under maximum generation conditions with no outages (N-0
contingency), as this represents the highest fault level. [Requirement 2 Part 2.3]
The assessment is conducted annually for the Near-Term planning horizon to ensure that the fault interrupting
devices can successfully interrupt the expected short circuit currents consistent with the Standard and
Guidelines for Short Circuit System Modeling and Short Circuit Assessment of The Southern Company Electric
Transmission System.

D. Interface Transfer Capability Assessments
Transfer capability assessments identify transmission facilities that may limit ITS Participants’ ability to
maintain long-term firm obligations across SBAA interfaces. Transfers are simulated incrementally in addition
to firm transactions modeled in base cases. To minimize sensitivity to local generation dispatch, transfers are
simulated by scaling load uniformly across participating areas. Transfer Distribution Factors (TDFs) and System
Operating Limits (SOLs) are considered when identifying limiting facilities.
Results, including assumptions, system models, and limiting facilities, are documented in a report provided to
Transmission Planning for inclusion in this document. Interfaces are evaluated annually to ensure the
Southern Balancing Authority meets all firm transmission commitments and reliability reserve margins.
All projects resulting from that analysis to address any identified deficiencies have been added to the list of
projects in Section IV D, Interface Transfer Capability Project Details.
Northern Interface
For the Northern interfaces with MISO, TVA, Duke Energy, Santee Cooper, and Dominion Energy – South
Carolina, transferring power across one interface may mutually impact the ability to transfer power across
other interfaces. Therefore, transfer capability assessments for the “northern” interfaces are evaluated in such
a way as to ensure not only that there is sufficient transfer capability to accommodate all firm transactions
across a particular interface, but also that there is sufficient transfer capability to accommodate all firm
obligations simultaneously across all the “northern” interfaces. Furthermore, these assessments do not
consider impacts due to transfer of directionally opposing flow(s) (i.e. “netting”). If transfers of opposing flow
are allowed to remain in the assessment cases, potential problems may be masked in certain real-time
situations when the transfers of opposing flow are not scheduled. Therefore, these opposing flow transfers
may be removed to ensure that the most conservative screens are performed.
Florida Interface
The SBAA – FRCC interface consists of ties with multiple companies within FRCC: Florida Power and Light
Company (FPL), DUKE Energy of Florida (DEF), JEA, and the City of Tallahassee (TAL); collectively “Florida.” It is
important to note that the Florida interface is fundamentally radial from the SBAA and the transmission
facilities in the connecting balancing authorities have a high-level of interdependence. To ensure the most
conservative screens are performed, impacts from “netting” are considered in the same manner as the

                                                              IV.       ANALYSIS RESULTS
A. Operating Guides
Operating guides are often a viable alternative to system improvements. When considering an operating
guide, factors such as operator action time and procedure complexity must be assessed to determine its
effectiveness in addressing the specific issue. If, for any reason, the use of an operating guide results in a
violation of the aforementioned risk assessment factors, then the operating guide is not used.
All operating guides identified and tested by Transmission Planning are reviewed by the Georgia Power
Transmission Operations team. The only exception occurs when an operating guide is developed for future use
after significant system upgrades, and Operations cannot replicate projected conditions.
Operating guides are re-evaluated during each planning cycle to confirm their continued appropriateness or to
determine if they should be replaced by a project. If a project is deemed more suitable, sufficient time must
be allowed for implementation.

F. Expansion Generation Units Details
The following projects are the result of the addition of Proxy Generation onto the ITS system.
The following information is included for each project:
    1) project justification,
    2) schedule for implementation (start date), and
    3) expected required in-service date.

For transmission improvements, start dates are established to allow sufficient lead time to meet the required
in-service date.

It is currently unknown where new generation resources will be located after 2029. To balance load and
generation in the base cases as demand grows and existing fossil units retire, assumptions must be made
regarding the locations of future generation assets. When creating cases, the expansion units listed in
Table 9 are included as needed. These sites are selected where fossil units have been or are expected to be
retired, as existing transmission connections are adequate and therefore expected to introduce minimal
additional constraints.


No projects were attributed to the expansion units included in the base cases as shown below.

                                              V.       ADDITIONAL SYSTEM ANALYSIS NOTES

Several additional studies are conducted throughout the year involving the Southern Company System as a
whole. These studies are performed by the Transmission Planning – Bulk Transmission Group and may result in
improvements to the Southern Company Transmission System, including the Georgia ITS. If system
enhancements are identified, their impacts are incorporated into the annual planning cycle.

A. Interface Analysis
    Interfaces within the Southern Balancing Authority Area (SBAA) are evaluated annually as part of the
    planning process. This analysis ensures that the SBAA can maintain all long-term firm transmission
    commitments and reliability reserve margins.

Northern Interface and Florida Interface Studies
   The Northern Interface Study and Florida Interface Study assess the import and export capability of these
   interfaces while ensuring compliance with long-term transmission commitments and reserve margins.
   When a transmission project is identified through an Interface Study, the recommendation is included in
   the analysis results referenced above.

B. Nuclear Final Safety Offsite Power Report (FSAR) Study
    The FSAR analysis is a requirement of the NUC-001 Nuclear Plant Interface Coordination for Southern
    Nuclear Operating Company and Transmission Planning. For GPC, this analysis is performed annually for
    Plant Vogtle and Plant Hatch and the results are communicated to Southern Nuclear.

C. Designation Studies
    Designation Studies identify transmission system improvements needed to provide firm transmission
    capability for resources designated to serve native load customers and wholesale network customers.

C. Strategic Projects
                                                       Cavender Drive - Wansley 500kV Line
                                                                  TEAMS 21496
                                                         Project Need Date: June 1, 2030
Executive Summary
The construction of the Cavender Drive – Wansley 500kV Line aims to address the evolving dynamics within the Georgia
Integrated Transmission System (ITS), primarily driven by the changes in generation and forecasted load growth. This
project involves the construction of a new ~37-mile 500 kV line from Cavender Drive to Wansley as shown on the figure
below.

The decision to undertake this project stems from the necessity to enhance available transmission capacity and mitigate
facility thermal constraints resulting from 500 kV contingencies under NERC TPL-001-5 (Category P1 – Single
Contingency Events). This project will reduce flows and increase available capacity on various circuits, thereby alleviating
or reducing thermal constraints on critical circuits under contingency scenarios.

                                                                         Figure 4 Area System Map

Compliance Statement
This project addresses problems associated with Category P1, EHV P2.3 and P3 events. These problems were identified
as part of Southern Company’s Transmission Planning process in compliance with NERC Standard TPL-001-5.

Background and Problem Description
The Cavender Drive – Wansley 500kV line effectively reduces flows and increases available capacity on circuits
overloaded above its facility rating shown in Table 1. Table 2 indicates capacity increases in relation to existing line
ratings for tie lines.

Discussion of Alternatives
The Preferred Plan ($      ) consists of:
    • Construction of the Cavender Drive - Wansley 500 kV Line (~37 miles) with (3) 100C 1113 ACSR conductor.
    • Expand Cavender Drive and Wansley Primary 500 kV yards to connect & terminate the new 500kV line.
    • Install necessary fiber and terminal protection and control equipment.

The preferred plan accomplishes the following:
    • High-Capacity Corridor: Establishes a new 500 kV line from Cavender Drive to Wansley, enhancing system
        capacity in the northwest area.
    • Reduced Flows, Increased Capacity: Decreases flows and increases available capacity on multiple circuits,
        improving system reliability.

Alternate Plans
    • Alternate Plan 1: Do Nothing ($ . Constraints in the system are required to be corrected for compliance with
        NERC Standard TPL-001-5.
    • Alternate Plan 2: Brute Force ($      ). This involves the direct replacement or rebuild of the facilities in Table
        1.

                                                                  Table 19 Brute Force Estimate

                                           Facility Name            Mileage Planning Grade Estimate
                             South Coweta 500/230kV Bank Addition    N/A           $
                             Dresden – Yates 230kV Rebuild           9.37         $
                             Villa Rica - Wansley 500kV Second Line   26         $
                                                Total                            $

          The main concern is to accommodate the necessary outages to facilitate construction activities along with
          maintaining system reliability.


Conclusion and Recommendations
The Cavender Drive – Wansley 500kV new line solves identified thermal constraints, provides additional 500kV corridor
for generation power transfers, and minimizes outage impacts to the transmission system during construction.

                    I.      GA INTEGRATED TRANSMISSION SYSTEM (ITS) EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

The results of the studies performed on the GA ITS demonstrate that required performance criteria are met,
or a project or operating guide has been developed to address any identified system deficiencies.
A summary of Georgia ITS Transmission additions starts on the next page, followed by the list of the Georgia
ITS 10-Year Expansion Plan Projects.
This group of projects and operating guides, found in Section IV ANALYSIS RESULTS, is reassessed annually to
confirm continued need, timing, and scope for previously identified projects until projects have transitioned
from planning to a committed project. These reassessments also identify any new potential projects needed
or modification to projects currently included. Any operating guides identified to address constraints are
reviewed by Georgia Power Company’s Transmission Operations team. The transmission improvements are
submitted to the ITS Participants for inclusion in the ITS parity process.
The following information is included for each project:
    1) project justification,
    2) implementation schedule (start date), and
    3) expected required in-service date.

For transmission improvements, lead times necessary to implement plans are considered to ensure the
expected required in-service date can be met.

                                    II.     TRANSMISSION PLANNING PROCESS DESCRIPTION

A. Annual Planning Process and Base Cases
Southern Company Services (SCS) conducts an iterative Transmission Planning process for the 10-year
planning horizon. This process ensures Georgia Integrated Transmission System (ITS) Participants receive all
necessary information to address identified system limitations. It enables them to develop projects that
comply with NERC planning standards and align with each participant’s budget and scheduling requirements.
The ITS Joint Committee for Planning and Operations determines which ITS Participant will assume
construction and ownership responsibilities, considering factors such as facility ownership and the ITS parity
forecast.

This report summarizes planning studies conducted by SCS specifically for the Georgia ITS in its role as
Planning Coordinator (PC) and Transmission Planner (TP). These studies follow the Guidelines for Planning
Transmission System Facility Improvements and are consistent with the NERC TPL-001-5 Standard
(“Standard”).

The following sections provide an overview of maintaining system models, the detailed studies performed,
which includes steady state, stability, and short circuit studies, and the resulting Projects and Operating
Guides for the mitigation of identified system deficiencies.


Maintaining System Models
The base cases include the following [Requirement 1]: Detailed studies are performed using transmission
system models (“base cases”) that are updated annually to reflect the current 10-year forecast for load and
generation within the Southern Balancing Authority Area (SBAA). These base cases use data consistent with
the NERC MOD-032 standard and are supplemented by other sources as needed, including items from the
Corrective Action Plan (CAP) and projected system conditions. Each base case also incorporates the latest
available external representation of the Eastern Interconnection, typically obtained from the Multi-Regional
Modeling Working Group (MMWG) or the SERC Reliability Corporation (SERC) Long-Term Study Group.

In accordance with [Requirement 1], the base cases include:
    1. Existing facilities.
    2. Known outages of generation or transmission facilities lasting at least six months. All such outages in
       the near-term Transmission Planning horizon are modeled with the impacted equipment out of
       service, as described in Attachment 1 of the MOD-032 Standard.
    3. New planned facilities and changes to existing facilities, rated per NERC Reliability Standard FAC-008-3.
    4. Real and reactive load forecasts provided by each Load Serving Entity within the SBAA.
    5. Known commitments for Firm Transmission Service and Interchange.
    6. Resources required to serve load.


2025 GA ITS Ten-Year Plan (2026-2035)                                                                                                              Page 29 of 336

future-year analyses.

Generation
Another key modeling assumption made in case development is the generation resources. Future generation
assumptions for native load resources for Southern Company, GTC, MEAG, and Dalton are shown in the table
in Section VI Generation Assumptions. This table lists both owned units and Power Purchase Agreements for
all parties at the beginning of the year. The dispatch program first commits sufficient resources to meet load
and reserve requirements for each company in each base case or unit-out scenario. It then adjusts generator
output levels in the most economical manner.

Normal Open Points
The ITS evaluates normal open point configurations on the Summer Cases. Some loads with radial service have
alternative transmission paths that can be used if the primary path is out of service. These alternative paths
cannot remain closed while the primary path is also closed because the resulting configuration would
compromise system protection and could create network load flow constraints.
If a change to a normal open point is requested, Operations and Planning will review the proposed
configuration to confirm that the system can accommodate the change before reconfiguration occurs.

                                                         III.     PERFORMANCE CRITERIA

A. Steady State Analysis
Steady state analyses were conducted to address TPL-001-5 Table 1 Category P0–P7 Planning Events and
Extreme Events for both near-term and long-term planning horizons. These evaluations included peak and off-
peak loading models. The System Peak loading model represents summer conditions. System Shoulder loading
models represent 85% of summer peak demand, with hydro generation motoring off-line, and include
scenarios where solar facilities are either on or off-line. This load assumption was anticipated to result in the
highest system stress outside of a full summer peak scenario, as many energy-limited resources were
projected to be off-line. Additionally, System Off-Peak cases representing 70% of the summer peak demand
were evaluated. All System Peak, Shoulder, and Off-Peak cases are evaluated using Rate B (95°F ambient
temperature) in accordance with [Requirement 2 Parts 2.1.1, 2.1.2, and 2.2.1].
A Hot Weather case representing 107% of system peak was also evaluated under ITS procedures using Rate A
(104°F ambient temperature) for all equipment ratings.
Based on these analyses, all projects required to address identified deficiencies have been added to Section
IV-E, Steady State Project Details.
Table 6 Steady State Transmission Planning Criteria below provides an overview of the methodology used to
meet TPL-001-5 Table 1 contingency requirements:

Where Table 6 Steady State Transmission Planning Criteria required a generation outage as a portion of the
contingency, a summary of key unit outs considered was developed and can be found in Section VI B,
Generation Assumptions. This table identifies the units considered and the cases in which they were applied.
Some outages were unnecessary in certain cases because the unit was already off-line due to expected
dispatch. These generating units, which impose greater stress on the system, have been identified through
years of power flow analysis based on factors such as size, location, and system impact.

Steady State Sensitivity Analysis
The standard requires sensitivity studies to demonstrate the impact of changes to base-case assumptions. The
selected sensitivity was the availability of hydroelectric generation, evaluated using TPL-001-5 Table 1 criteria.
Analyses were performed for all years in the Near-Term and Long-Term Planning Horizons under off-peak
conditions with hydro generation available and under System Shoulder conditions (85% of system peak) with
hydro generation unavailable. [Requirement 2 Part 2.1.4]

Steady State Equipment Sparing Analysis
The Transmission Equipment Sparing Strategy is reviewed annually to identify transmission equipment
without a spare and with a replacement lead time greater than one year. Each piece of equipment was
individually modeled as unavailable and evaluated for P0, P1, and P2 events using system peak, off-peak, and
the sensitivity cases. [Requirement 2 Part 2.1.5]

B. Stability Analysis
Stability studies were conducted to consider P1 - P7 Planning Events and Extreme Events in the Near-Term
planning horizon. Simulations were conducted for system peak load and off-peak load (approximately 50% of
peak) for one of the five Near-Term years. System Peak cases included a dynamic load model representing
expected induction motor behavior. The light load level of 50% of peak was chosen as a worst-case scenario
for angular stability because base-load units operate at maximum output.
All projects resulting from the stability analysis to address any identified deficiencies have been added to the
list of projects in Section IV B, Stability Project Details.

methodology to meet TPL-001-5 Table 1 performance requirements:

Stability Sensitivity Analysis (Near-Term Planning Horizon)
Requirement R2.4.3 of the Standard requires additional sensitivity studies to demonstrate the effects of
various modeling assumptions. For the system stability studies completed using the standard base case, the
following sensitivities were evaluated:

    •     For 50% System peak load cases, local generation was increased to maximum output.
    •     For System peak load cases, the percentage of induction motor load that was modeled at each bus
          with a dynamic load model was increased.

For studies evaluating area generator output sensitivity, generator output was modified beyond the base
dispatch, dispatching all generation near the study area at full output, whether the unit had firm service for
full output or not. This approach produced the most conservative results; therefore, no additional sensitivities
were required. The sensitivity analysis revealed no new constraints. [Requirement R2.4.3]

Steady State Coordination with Adjacent Systems
In addition to contingencies on the GA ITS system, contingencies provided by neighboring systems are
analyzed annually in accordance with TPL-001-5 Requirement 3.4.1. Neighboring systems are monitored
during all studies to determine if ITS contingencies could impact them. If potential impacts are identified, the
affected neighbor is notified per the requirement.

Long-Term Stability Analysis
Stability studies were also conducted as needed in the Long-Term planning horizon to address the impact of
material generation additions or changes in that time frame. Forecasted generation in the Long-Term
transmission planning horizon that does not have firm service or has not been designated by an entity does
not require a stability study. Only new generation with a firm commitment to build requires a unit-specific
stability study. [Requirement 2.5]

C. Short Circuit Analysis
The short circuit (breaker duty) assessment was performed by Southern Company Services Protection &
Control Applications for the Near-Term planning horizon. The base case model used for this assessment
included all existing facilities (transmission and generation) and planned facilities based on forecasted
generation and future years’ transmission expansion plan. The real and reactive load forecasts and known
commitments for Firm Transmission Service and Interchange were not represented in the models as they were
not relevant to this assessment. The methodology uses the Siemens APA “Advanced Protection Assessment”
Short Circuit Analysis program to calculate the margin between fault interrupting device capability and short
circuit levels. Short circuit currents are evaluated under maximum generation conditions with no outages (N-0
contingency), as this represents the highest fault level. [Requirement 2 Part 2.3]
The assessment is conducted annually for the Near-Term planning horizon to ensure that the fault interrupting
devices can successfully interrupt the expected short circuit currents consistent with the Standard and
Guidelines for Short Circuit System Modeling and Short Circuit Assessment of The Southern Company Electric
Transmission System.

All projects resulting from that analysis to address any identified deficiencies have been added to the list of

D. Interface Transfer Capability Assessments
Transfer capability assessments identify transmission facilities that may limit ITS Participants’ ability to
maintain long-term firm obligations across SBAA interfaces. Transfers are simulated incrementally in addition
to firm transactions modeled in base cases. To minimize sensitivity to local generation dispatch, transfers are
simulated by scaling load uniformly across participating areas. Transfer Distribution Factors (TDFs) and System
Operating Limits (SOLs) are considered when identifying limiting facilities.
Results, including assumptions, system models, and limiting facilities, are documented in a report provided to
Transmission Planning for inclusion in this document. Interfaces are evaluated annually to ensure the
Southern Balancing Authority meets all firm transmission commitments and reliability reserve margins.
All projects resulting from that analysis to address any identified deficiencies have been added to the list of
projects in Section IV D, Interface Transfer Capability Project Details.
Northern Interface
For the Northern interfaces with MISO, TVA, Duke Energy, Santee Cooper, and Dominion Energy – South
Carolina, transferring power across one interface may mutually impact the ability to transfer power across
other interfaces. Therefore, transfer capability assessments for the “northern” interfaces are evaluated in such
a way as to ensure not only that there is sufficient transfer capability to accommodate all firm transactions
across a particular interface, but also that there is sufficient transfer capability to accommodate all firm
obligations simultaneously across all the “northern” interfaces. Furthermore, these assessments do not
consider impacts due to transfer of directionally opposing flow(s) (i.e. “netting”). If transfers of opposing flow
are allowed to remain in the assessment cases, potential problems may be masked in certain real-time
situations when the transfers of opposing flow are not scheduled. Therefore, these opposing flow transfers
may be removed to ensure that the most conservative screens are performed.
Florida Interface
The SBAA – FRCC interface consists of ties with multiple companies within FRCC: Florida Power and Light
Company (FPL), DUKE Energy of Florida (DEF), JEA, and the City of Tallahassee (TAL); collectively “Florida.” It is
important to note that the Florida interface is fundamentally radial from the SBAA and the transmission
facilities in the connecting balancing authorities have a high-level of interdependence. To ensure the most
conservative screens are performed, impacts from “netting” are considered in the same manner as the

                                                              IV.       ANALYSIS RESULTS
A. Operating Guides
Operating guides are often a viable alternative to system improvements. When considering an operating
guide, factors such as operator action time and procedure complexity must be assessed to determine its
effectiveness in addressing the specific issue. If, for any reason, the use of an operating guide results in a
violation of the aforementioned risk assessment factors, then the operating guide is not used.
All operating guides identified and tested by Transmission Planning are reviewed by the Georgia Power
Transmission Operations team. The only exception occurs when an operating guide is developed for future use
after significant system upgrades, and Operations cannot replicate projected conditions.
Operating guides are re-evaluated during each planning cycle to confirm their continued appropriateness or to
determine if they should be replaced by a project. If a project is deemed more suitable, sufficient time must
be allowed for implementation.

F. Expansion Generation Units Details
The following projects are the result of the addition of Proxy Generation onto the ITS system.
The following information is included for each project:
    1) project justification,
    2) schedule for implementation (start date), and
    3) expected required in-service date.

For transmission improvements, start dates are established to allow sufficient lead time to meet the required
in-service date.

It is currently unknown where new generation resources will be located after 2029. To balance load and
generation in the base cases as demand grows and existing fossil units retire, assumptions must be made
regarding the locations of future generation assets. When creating cases, the expansion units listed in
Table 9 are included as needed. These sites are selected where fossil units have been or are expected to be
retired, as existing transmission connections are adequate and therefore expected to introduce minimal
additional constraints.


No projects were attributed to the expansion units included in the base cases as shown below.

                                              V.       ADDITIONAL SYSTEM ANALYSIS NOTES

Several additional studies are conducted throughout the year involving the Southern Company System as a
whole. These studies are performed by the Transmission Planning – Bulk Transmission Group and may result in
improvements to the Southern Company Transmission System, including the Georgia ITS. If system
enhancements are identified, their impacts are incorporated into the annual planning cycle.

A. Interface Analysis
    Interfaces within the Southern Balancing Authority Area (SBAA) are evaluated annually as part of the
    planning process. This analysis ensures that the SBAA can maintain all long-term firm transmission
    commitments and reliability reserve margins.

Northern Interface and Florida Interface Studies
   The Northern Interface Study and Florida Interface Study assess the import and export capability of these
   interfaces while ensuring compliance with long-term transmission commitments and reserve margins.
   When a transmission project is identified through an Interface Study, the recommendation is included in
   the analysis results referenced above.

B. Nuclear Final Safety Offsite Power Report (FSAR) Study
    The FSAR analysis is a requirement of the NUC-001 Nuclear Plant Interface Coordination for Southern
    Nuclear Operating Company and Transmission Planning. For GPC, this analysis is performed annually for
    Plant Vogtle and Plant Hatch and the results are communicated to Southern Nuclear.

C. Designation Studies
    Designation Studies identify transmission system improvements needed to provide firm transmission
    capability for resources designated to serve native load customers and wholesale network customers.

C. Strategic Projects
                                                       Cavender Drive - Wansley 500kV Line
                                                                  TEAMS 21496
                                                         Project Need Date: June 1, 2030
Executive Summary
The construction of the Cavender Drive – Wansley 500kV Line aims to address the evolving dynamics within the Georgia
Integrated Transmission System (ITS), primarily driven by the changes in generation and forecasted load growth. This
project involves the construction of a new ~37-mile 500 kV line from Cavender Drive to Wansley as shown on the figure
below.

The decision to undertake this project stems from the necessity to enhance available transmission capacity and mitigate
facility thermal constraints resulting from 500 kV contingencies under NERC TPL-001-5 (Category P1 – Single
Contingency Events). This project will reduce flows and increase available capacity on various circuits, thereby alleviating
or reducing thermal constraints on critical circuits under contingency scenarios.

                                                                         Figure 4 Area System Map

Compliance Statement
This project addresses problems associated with Category P1, EHV P2.3 and P3 events. These problems were identified
as part of Southern Company’s Transmission Planning process in compliance with NERC Standard TPL-001-5.

Background and Problem Description
The Cavender Drive – Wansley 500kV line effectively reduces flows and increases available capacity on circuits
overloaded above its facility rating shown in Table 1. Table 2 indicates capacity increases in relation to existing line
ratings for tie lines.

Discussion of Alternatives
The Preferred Plan ($      ) consists of:
    • Construction of the Cavender Drive - Wansley 500 kV Line (~37 miles) with (3) 100C 1113 ACSR conductor.
    • Expand Cavender Drive and Wansley Primary 500 kV yards to connect & terminate the new 500kV line.
    • Install necessary fiber and terminal protection and control equipment.

The preferred plan accomplishes the following:
    • High-Capacity Corridor: Establishes a new 500 kV line from Cavender Drive to Wansley, enhancing system
        capacity in the northwest area.
    • Reduced Flows, Increased Capacity: Decreases flows and increases available capacity on multiple circuits,
        improving system reliability.

Alternate Plans
    • Alternate Plan 1: Do Nothing ($ . Constraints in the system are required to be corrected for compliance with
        NERC Standard TPL-001-5.
    • Alternate Plan 2: Brute Force ($      ). This involves the direct replacement or rebuild of the facilities in Table
        1.

                                                                  Table 19 Brute Force Estimate

                                           Facility Name            Mileage Planning Grade Estimate
                             South Coweta 500/230kV Bank Addition    N/A           $
                             Dresden – Yates 230kV Rebuild           9.37         $
                             Villa Rica - Wansley 500kV Second Line   26         $
                                                Total                            $

          The main concern is to accommodate the necessary outages to facilitate construction activities along with
          maintaining system reliability.


Conclusion and Recommendations
The Cavender Drive – Wansley 500kV new line solves identified thermal constraints, provides additional 500kV corridor
for generation power transfers, and minimizes outage impacts to the transmission system during construction.
